Variance Components with Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals

Source: R/varcomp.R
varcomp.Rd

The variance components of a fitted model, with standard errors and confidence intervals, for every model class that predictmeans handles: the random-effect variances and covariances and the residual variance of lmer, lme and glmmTMB models (also with correlation and variance structures and random slopes), the random-effect (co)variances of glmer models, the correlation and variance-function parameters of gls and lme models, the stratum variance components of aov models with Error(), the smoothing variance components of mgcv::gam models and semireg fits, and the error term of lm, aov and glm models (residual variance, dispersion, or the negative binomial \(\theta\)).

Usage

varcomp(model, ci = TRUE, conf_level = 0.95,
        ci_method = c("Satterthwaite", "Wald", "profile"),
        information = c("observed", "average", "expected"), test = FALSE,
        test_method = c("auto", "mixture", "bootstrap"), nsim = 10000, nboot = 999,
        ncore = 1, ...)

Arguments

model

A fitted model (see Description).

ci

TRUE (the default): add confidence intervals.

conf_level

Confidence level of the intervals; the default is 0.95 (level before 2.0).

...

Not used: level (before 2.0) stops with its 2.0 spelling.

ci_method

How the intervals of variances are made: "Satterthwaite" (the default) chi-square intervals with \(\nu = 2 (estimate/SE)^2\) df, as SAS PROC MIXED (COVTEST CL); "Wald" Wald intervals on the log scale; "profile" (lmer, glmer) lme4's profile-likelihood intervals, which for a REML fit are those of the ML fit (lme4 profiles the ML deviance), so they do not go with the REML estimates. The other components always get the Wald intervals of the Details.

information

For REML fits of lmer, lme and gls models: the information matrix of the variance parameters behind the SEs: "observed" (the default, as SAS PROC MIXED), "average" (the average information of Genstat's and ASReml's REML: Genstat's s.e.) or "expected"; the same choices as for the Kenward-Roger df (df_method of predictmeans). Other fits use the observed information.

test

TRUE: add a likelihood ratio test of each component being zero (lmer, glmer, glmmTMB and semireg fits; see ‘Tests’). The default is FALSE: each test refits the model once.

test_method

"auto" (the default) or "mixture": the reference distribution of a single variance (see ‘Tests’); "bootstrap": a parametric bootstrap of each likelihood ratio, for small samples, few levels, or where the asymptotic references are conservative.

nsim

Number of draws of the exact null distribution of the restricted likelihood ratio (default 10000, with a fixed seed, so the p-values repeat).

nboot

Maximum number of bootstrap samples per test (default 999); a test stops early once 20 simulated statistics reach the observed one.

ncore

Number of cores for the bootstrap (default 1; a socket cluster on Windows). The p-values are the same for any ncore.

Value

A data frame with one row per component (random-effect variances and covariances by group, named group.term and group.term1.term2; correlation and variance-function parameters named cor.name and var.name; residual) and columns vcov (the estimate), SE and, with ci = TRUE, the limits. Values are rounded to 4 decimals; attribute "ci_method" says how the intervals were made. With test = TRUE also LRT and p.value, and class "pm_varcomp" (printed with the hypotheses). Notes on this fit (e.g. a variance estimated at zero, few levels) are kept in attr(, "advice"); read them with advice.

Details

Standard errors are from the observed information of the variance parameters (the inverse Hessian of the REML, or ML, deviance at the estimates, as SAS PROC MIXED and the Kenward-Roger df of predictmeans), carried to the variance components by the delta method: lmer from the deviance in (theta, sigma), glmer from the Hessian lme4 stores for (theta, beta) (nAGQ = 0 fits: the deviance in theta), lme and gls from the REML (ML) log-likelihood in their unconstrained modelStruct parameters (any pdMat, corStruct and varFunc), glmmTMB from vcov(full = TRUE).

Intervals of variances: Satterthwaite's chi-square interval \([\nu \hat\sigma^2/\chi^2_{\nu, 1-\alpha/2}, \nu \hat\sigma^2/\chi^2_{\nu, \alpha/2}]\) with \(\nu = 2 (\hat\sigma^2/SE)^2\) (positive and skewed as the sampling distribution of a variance; for the residual variance of an lm it is the exact interval, \(\nu\) the residual df; for the stratum components of an aov Satterthwaite's interval from the mean squares). Other components: Wald intervals on the scale where the parameter is unbounded: atanh for correlations (a covariance: the interval of its correlation times the two SDs), log for other positive parameters (varIdent ratios, ranges, \(\theta\)), and the natural scale otherwise (e.g. the power of varPower). A variance estimated at its bound, zero, has no SE (the interval is (0, NA)), as SAS prints it; an analysis of variance estimate can be negative.

lm, aov, gaussian glm: the residual variance \(s^2\) with SE \(s^2 \sqrt{2/df}\) and the exact chi-square interval. Other glm families with an estimated dispersion (Gamma, inverse gaussian, quasi): the Pearson dispersion, with the same (approximate) SE and interval. Poisson and binomial: the dispersion is fixed at 1 (no SE). Negative binomial (MASS::glm.nb): \(\theta\) with its SE.

aov with Error(): the analysis of variance (method of moments) estimates of the variance of each error stratum, from the stratum mean squares and their expectations (as Genstat's stratum variances; they equal the REML estimates in balanced designs when positive, and can be negative), with SEs from \(var(MS) = 2 MS^2/df\) and Satterthwaite's chi-square intervals; with missing values, those of the design completed as in predictmeans.

gam: mgcv::gam.vcomp() (variances of the smooths, and the scale), its intervals squared, and the SEs from their width on the log scale; it needs method = "REML" or "ML".

Tests

With test = TRUE each row gets the likelihood ratio test of the model one would fit without it (columns LRT and p.value; the hypotheses and reference distributions are printed below the table and kept in attr(, "tests")):

RowModel refittedReference distribution
variance of a one-variance term (1 | g), smooth blockthe term dropped\(\frac12\chi^2_0 + \frac12\chi^2_1\); exact restricted LRT when it is the only random effect of a gaussian lmer/semireg REML fit
slope variance in (1 + x | g) (k components)(1 | g)\(\frac12\chi^2_{k-1} + \frac12\chi^2_k\)
intercept variance of (1 + x | g), variance of ar1() etc.the whole term dropped\(\chi^2\) with the term's number of parameters (conservative)
covariance in (1 + x | g)(1 + x || g) (glmmTMB: diag())\(\chi^2\) with the number of covariances
correlation of ar1(), ou(), cs()homdiag() / diag()\(\chi^2_1\)
residual variance; a structure that is the residual covariance (dispformula = ~0)no test

A variance is on the boundary of its range under the hypothesis, so its likelihood ratio has the mixture distributions of Self and Liang (1987) and Stram and Lee (1994), not \(\chi^2_1\) (which is conservative, as lmerTest::ranova()). When the tested variance is the only random effect of a gaussian model fitted by REML, the exact finite-sample null distribution of Crainiceanu and Ruppert (2004) is used (simulated); with other random effects present that distribution is no longer exact (in simulations it was too liberal), and the mixture is used. The mixture p-values equal SAS PROC GLIMMIX COVTEST, the likelihood ratios SAS PROC MIXED and Genstat REML (tests/testthat/test-vc-test.R). Where a p-value may be inaccurate in either direction (a term with fewer than 6 levels; binary data with fewer than 5 observations per level, where the Laplace approximation is poor), a warning names the rows and suggests the bootstrap.

test_method = "bootstrap": for each test, responses are simulated from the model without the component (new random effects and errors), both models are refitted to each, and the p-value is \((\#\{LRT^* \ge LRT\} + 1)/(b + 1)\). It needs no distributional approximation, so it is the check for the rows the warning names. A test stops once 20 simulated statistics reach the observed one (Besag and Clifford 1991): a clearly non-significant row needs some 40-400 refits, a significant one all nboot pairs. Each draw has its own seed, so the p-values repeat, with or without ncore. Run time: a few seconds to a minute for usual lmer and glmer models; glmmTMB fits are slower (each refit rebuilds the model). For lme, gls, gam and models without random effects test = TRUE is not available.

Which method: in a simulation of seven designs (dev/sim-vc-defaults.R in the package sources) the default rejected at most 4.5% of the data sets without the component at the 5% level: it was never liberal. For GLMMs it was conservative (binary data in clusters of four 0.5%, Poisson 4%, negative binomial 0%), and there the bootstrap rejected 1.5-6% and found 5-7% more of the real components. Use the default for gaussian models and as a quick first look; use the bootstrap for GLMMs, small data sets, the rows a warning names, and a p-value near the cut-off.

References

Besag, J. and Clifford, P. (1991). Sequential Monte Carlo p-values. Biometrika, 78, 301-304.

Crainiceanu, C. M. and Ruppert, D. (2004). Likelihood ratio tests in linear mixed models with one variance component. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 66, 165-185.

Self, S. G. and Liang, K.-Y. (1987). Asymptotic properties of maximum likelihood estimators and likelihood ratio tests under nonstandard conditions. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 82, 605-610.

Stram, D. O. and Lee, J. W. (1994). Variance components testing in the longitudinal mixed effects model. Biometrics, 50, 1171-1177.

See also

anova.semireg, R2_model, se_ranef, advice

Author

Dongwen Luo, Siva Ganesh and John Koolaard

Examples

library(predictmeans)
Oats$nitro <- factor(Oats$nitro)
fm <- lmer(yield ~ nitro*Variety+(1|Block/Variety), data=Oats)
varcomp(fm)
#>                               vcov       SE    2.5 %    97.5 %
#> Variety:Block.(Intercept) 106.0618  67.8754  40.9773  657.7703
#> Block.(Intercept)         214.4810 168.8381  70.8628 2575.3156
#> residual                  177.0831  37.3324 121.8272  280.9241
# is each variance needed? (one refit per row)
varcomp(fm, test = TRUE)
#>                               vcov       SE    2.5 %    97.5 %    LRT  p.value
#> Variety:Block.(Intercept) 106.0618  67.8754  40.9773  657.7703 7.6615 0.002821
#> Block.(Intercept)         214.4810 168.8381  70.8628 2575.3156 4.9782 0.012830
#> residual                  177.0831  37.3324 121.8272  280.9241     NA       NA
#> 
#> Tests (likelihood ratio, each row's model refitted):
#>   Variety:Block.(Intercept): drop (1 | Variety:Block); 0.5 chi2(0) + 0.5 chi2(1)
#>   Block.(Intercept): drop (1 | Block); 0.5 chi2(0) + 0.5 chi2(1)
# \donttest{
# the same by parametric bootstrap (a few seconds; more draws and ncore for real use)
varcomp(fm, test = TRUE, test_method = "bootstrap", nboot = 99)
#>                               vcov       SE    2.5 %    97.5 %    LRT p.value
#> Variety:Block.(Intercept) 106.0618  67.8754  40.9773  657.7703 7.6615    0.01
#> Block.(Intercept)         214.4810 168.8381  70.8628 2575.3156 4.9782    0.02
#> residual                  177.0831  37.3324 121.8272  280.9241     NA      NA
#> 
#> Tests (likelihood ratio, each row's model refitted):
#>   Variety:Block.(Intercept): drop (1 | Variety:Block); parametric bootstrap (99 draws)
#>   Block.(Intercept): drop (1 | Block); parametric bootstrap (99 draws)
# }
# a GLMM: the boundary mixture is conservative here, the bootstrap nearer 5%
gm <- glmer(cbind(incidence, size - incidence) ~ period + (1 | herd),
            family = binomial, data = lme4::cbpp)
varcomp(gm, test = TRUE)
#>                    vcov     SE  2.5 % 97.5 %     LRT   p.value
#> herd.(Intercept) 0.4125 0.2294 0.1757 1.8476 14.0058 9.112e-05
#> 
#> Tests (likelihood ratio, each row's model refitted):
#>   herd.(Intercept): drop (1 | herd); 0.5 chi2(0) + 0.5 chi2(1)
fm1 <- lme(yield ~ nitro*Variety, random=~1|Block/Variety, data=Oats)
varcomp(fm1)
#>                         vcov       SE    2.5 %    97.5 %
#> Block.(Intercept)   214.4745 168.8318  70.8610 2575.1692
#> Variety.(Intercept) 106.0618  67.8756  40.9772  657.7746
#> residual            177.0835  37.3325 121.8275  280.9250
# the same components by the analysis of variance
varcomp(aov(yield ~ nitro*Variety + Error(Block/Variety), data=Oats))
#>                   vcov       SE    2.5 %    97.5 %
#> Block         214.4771 168.8340  70.8619 2575.2100
#> Block:Variety 106.0618  67.8755  40.9773  657.7726
#> residual      177.0833  37.3324 121.8274  280.9246

data(Orthodont, package="nlme")
mod1 <- lme(distance ~ age, random=~age|Subject, data=Orthodont)
varcomp(mod1)
#>                            vcov     SE   2.5 %   97.5 %
#> Subject.(Intercept)      5.4151 4.9583  1.5819 128.6996
#> Subject.age.(Intercept) -0.3211 0.4244 -0.4943   0.1570
#> Subject.age              0.0513 0.0415  0.0166   0.6844
#> residual                 1.7162 0.3303  1.2163   2.6042
# correlation and variance structures
mod2 <- gls(distance ~ age*Sex, correlation=corAR1(form=~1|Subject),
            weights=varIdent(form=~1|Sex), data=Orthodont)
varcomp(mod2)
#>              vcov     SE  2.5 %  97.5 %
#> cor.Phi    0.7473 0.0681 0.5815  0.8535
#> var.Female 0.5647 0.0908 0.4121  0.7738
#> residual   9.5035 2.8443 5.7032 18.9234
# the error term of a linear model
varcomp(lm(yield ~ Block + nitro*Variety, data=Oats))
#>              vcov      SE    2.5 %   97.5 %
#> residual 254.2192 48.4777 180.6923 384.1423
